L222: DeepSeek Harness (`dsh`) is an open-source agent harness developed by cite127†DeepSeek AI†deepseek.com .

L238:     npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web
L239: 
L240: The command starts the Web UI at `http://127.0.0.1:3080` by default and opens it in the default browser for a local launch. L83: Some tool operations may be sensitive and require human approval before execution. Deep Agents support human-in-the-loop workflows through LangGraph’s interrupt capabilities. You can configure which tools require approval using the `interrupt_on` parameter. When `interrupt_on` is set, `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware` is added to the cite43†Deep Agents stack .
L84: If a run is cancelled or interrupted before a tool returns a result, cite44†`PatchToolCallsMiddleware`†reference.langchain.com in the same stack repairs the message history automatically.

L89: Basic configuration
L90: 
L91: The `interrupt_on` parameter accepts a dictionary mapping tool names to interrupt configurations. Each tool can be configured with:
L92:   * `True`: Enable interrupts with default behavior (approve, edit, reject, respond allowed)
L93:   * `False`: Disable interrupts for this tool
L94:   * `InterruptOnConfig`: Custom configuration. Set `allowed_decisions` to control review options. In Python, add an optional `when` predicate to interrupt only specific calls (see cite46†Conditional interrupts ).

L377: ✅ `approve`  | Execute the tool with the original arguments as proposed by the agent.  | Send an email draft exactly as written
L378: ✏️ `edit`  | Modify the tool arguments before execution.  | Change the recipient before sending an email
L379: ❌ `reject`  | Skip executing this tool call entirely and return rejection feedback to the agent.  | Deny file deletion and explain why
L380: 💬 `respond`  | Return the human’s message directly as a synthetic tool result, skipping execution, for “ask user” style tools.  | Answer an `"ask_user"` prompt with a direct reply
L381: Use `reject` when the human denies a proposed action. Use `respond` only when the human is acting as the tool, such as answering an `ask_user` prompt. Do not use `respond` to deny side-effecting tools, because its message may be treated by the model as a successful tool result.
L382: When editing tool arguments, make changes conservatively. Significant modifications to the original arguments may cause the model to re-evaluate its approach and potentially execute the tool multiple times or take unexpected actions.

L582: The `namespace` parameter controls data isolation. For multi-user deployments, always set a cite64†namespace factory to isolate data per user or tenant.

L584: How it works:
L585: 
L586:   * cite65†`StoreBackend`†reference.langchain.com stores files in a LangGraph cite66†`BaseStore`†reference.langchain.com provided by the runtime, enabling cross‑thread durable storage.

L589:   * When you’re deploying your agent through cite49†LangSmith Deployment (a store is automatically provisioned for your agent).
L590: ####
L591: 
L592: cite64†​ L593: 
L594: Namespace factories
L595: 
L596: A namespace factory controls where `StoreBackend` reads and writes data. It receives a LangGraph cite67†`Runtime`†reference.langchain.com and returns a tuple of strings used as the store namespace. Use namespace factories to isolate data between users, tenants, or assistants. Pass the namespace factory to the `namespace` parameter when constructing a `StoreBackend`:
L597: 
L598:     `NamespaceFactory = Callable[[Runtime], tuple[str, ...]]
L599:     `
L600: 
L601: The `Runtime` provides:
L602:   * `rt.context`—User-supplied context passed via LangGraph’s cite68†context schema†langchain-ai.github.io (for example, `user_id`)
L603:   * `rt.server_info`—Server-specific metadata when running on LangGraph Server (assistant ID, graph ID, authenticated user)
L604:   * `rt.execution_info`—Execution identity information (thread ID, run ID, checkpoint ID)
L605: The `Runtime` argument is available in `deepagents>=0.5.2`. Earlier 0.5.x releases passed a `BackendContext` instead—see cite69†migrating from `BackendContext` below. `rt.server_info` and `rt.execution_info` require `deepagents>=0.5.0`.
L606: Common namespace patterns:
L607: 
L608:     `from deepagents.backends import StoreBackend
L609: 
L610:     # Per-user: each user gets their own isolated storage
L611:     backend = StoreBackend(
L612:         namespace=lambda rt: (rt.server_info.user.identity,),
L613:     )
L614: 
L615:     # Per-assistant: all users of the same assistant share storage
L616:     backend = StoreBackend(
L617:         namespace=lambda rt: (
L618:             rt.server_info.assistant_id,
L619:         ),
L620:     )
L621: 
L622:     # Per-thread: storage scoped to a single conversation
L623:     backend = StoreBackend(
L624:         namespace=lambda rt: (
L625:             rt.execution_info.thread_id,
L626:         ),
L627:     )
L628:     `
L629: You can combine multiple components to create more specific scopes—for example, `(user_id, thread_id)` for per-user per-conversation isolation, or append a suffix like `"filesystem"` to disambiguate when the same scope uses multiple store namespaces. Namespace components must contain only alphanumeric characters, hyphens, underscores, dots, `@`, `+`, colons, and tildes. Wildcards (`*`, `?`) are rejected to prevent glob injection.
L630: The `namespace` parameter will be required in v0.5.0. Always set it explicitly for new code.
L631: 
L632: When no namespace factory is provided, the legacy default uses the `assistant_id` from LangGraph config metadata. This means all users of the same cite70†assistant share the same storage. For multi-user cite71†going to production , always provide a namespace factory.

L637: ContextHubBackend
L638: 
L639: Before you begin: `ContextHubBackend` requires a Context Hub repo set up in LangSmith. Read the cite72†Context Hub concepts page first if you’re unfamiliar with agent repos and skill repos.
L640: `ContextHubBackend` stores your agent’s filesystem in a LangSmith Context Hub repo. It can use a standalone repo or an agent repo that links out to skill repos. Repo structure: In the Context Hub, an agent repo holds the agent’s top-level instructions and configuration (for example, `AGENTS.md`, `tools.json`). It can link to one or more skill repos, each packaged as a reusable capability (for example, a `SKILL.md` with instructions for email formatting or code review).
L641: When you pass `ContextHubBackend("my-agent")`, the backend mounts the agent repo at the filesystem root; linked skill repos appear as subdirectories under `/skills/`. This means your agent’s context is intentionally spread across repos: one repo per agent, separate repos per skill. That separation lets skills be versioned, shared, and reused across multiple agents independently. If this feels fragmented, see cite73†Linked repos for the rationale.

L1119: Migrating from `BackendContext`
L1120: 
L1121: In `deepagents>=0.5.2` (Python) and `deepagents>=1.9.1` (TypeScript), namespace factories receive a LangGraph cite67†`Runtime`†reference.langchain.com directly instead of a `BackendContext` wrapper. The old `BackendContext` form still works via backwards-compatible `.runtime` and `.state` accessors, but those accessors emit a deprecation warning and will be removed in `deepagents>=0.7`. What changed:
L1122:   * The factory argument is now a `Runtime`, not a `BackendContext`.
L1123:   * Drop the `.runtime` accessor—for example, `ctx.runtime.context.user_id` becomes `rt.server_info.user.identity`.
L1124:   * There is no direct replacement for `ctx.state`. Namespace info should be read-only and stable for the lifetime of a run, whereas state is mutable and changes step-to-step—deriving a namespace from it risks data ending up under inconsistent keys. If you have a use case that requires reading agent state, please cite84†open an issue†github.com .

L152: ##
L153: 
L154: cite47†​ L155: 
L156: Stream messages
L157: Deep Agents can emit messages from the coordinator agent and from delegated subagents. Use `stream.messages` for top-level messages and `subagent.messages` for each delegated subagent.
L158: 
L159:     `stream = agent.stream_events(input, version="v3")
L160: 
L161:     coordinator_messages: list[str] = []
L162:     for message in stream.messages:
L163:         print("[coordinator]", message.text)
L164:         coordinator_messages.append(message.text)
L165: 
L166:     for subagent in stream.subagents:
L167:         for message in subagent.messages:
L168:             print(f"[{subagent.name}]", message.text)
L169:     `
L170: ##
L171: 
L172: cite48†​ L173: 
L174: Stream tool calls
L175: Deep Agents expose tool calls at each level of the agent tree. Use the top-level `stream.tool_calls` for coordinator tools and each `subagent.tool_calls` for delegated work.
L176: 
L177:     `stream = agent.stream_events(input, version="v3")
L178: 
L179:     coordinator_tool_names: list[str] = []
L180:     for call in stream.tool_calls:
L181:         print("[coordinator tool]", call.tool_name, call.input)
L182:         print(call.completed, call.error)
L183:         coordinator_tool_names.append(call.tool_name)
L184:     for subagent in stream.subagents:
L185:         for call in subagent.tool_calls:
L186:             print(f"[{subagent.name} tool]", call.tool_name, call.input)
L187:             for delta in call.output_deltas:
L188:                 print(delta, end="", flush=True)
L189: 
L190:             if call.completed and call.error is None:
L191:                 print(call.output)
L192:             elif call.error is not None:
L193:                 print(call.error)
L194:     `
L195: ##
L196: 
L197: cite49†​ L198: 
L199: Stream nested work
L200: You can recurse into a subagent stream to observe nested subagents, messages, and tool calls.
L201: 
L202:     `stream = agent.stream_events(input, version="v3")
L203: 
L204:     subagent_names: list[str] = []
L205:     for subagent in stream.subagents:
L206:         print(f"subagent {subagent.name}: {subagent.status}")
L207: 
L208:         for tool_call in subagent.tool_calls:
L209:             print(f"{tool_call.tool_name}({tool_call.input})")
L210:             for delta in tool_call.output_deltas:
L211:                 print(delta, end="", flush=True)
L212:         for nested in subagent.subagents:
L213:             print(f"nested subagent {nested.name}: {nested.status}")
L214: 
L215:         subagent_names.append(subagent.name)
L216:     `

L219: cite50†​ L220: 
L221: Consume concurrently
L222: Coordinator and subagent output often interleave. Consume projections concurrently when you need live UI updates. For concurrent consumption in async code, use `astream_events` with `asyncio.gather`:
L223: 
L224:     `import asyncio
L225: 
L226:     stream = await agent.astream_events(input, version="v3")
L227: 
L228:     async def consume_coordinator():
L229:         async for message in stream.messages:
L230:             print("[coordinator]", await message.text)
L231: 
L232:     async def consume_subagents():
L233:         async for subagent in stream.subagents:
L234:             async for message in subagent.messages:
L235:                 print(f"[{subagent.name}]", await message.text)
L236: 
L237:     await asyncio.gather(consume_coordinator(), consume_subagents())
L238:     `
L239: For synchronous code, use `stream.interleave(...)` instead:
L240: 
L241:     `stream = agent.stream_events(input, version="v3")
L242: 
L243:     for name, item in stream.interleave("messages", "subagents"):
L244:         if name == "messages":
L245:             print("[coordinator]", item.text)
L246:         else:
L247:             for message in item.messages:
L248:                 print(f"[{item.name}]", message.text)
L249:     `
L250: When you need exact arrival order across the coordinator and all subagents, iterate raw protocol events and use `namespace` to identify the source:
L251: 
L252:     `stream = agent.stream_events(input, version="v3")
L253: 
L254:     text_deltas: list[str] = []
L255:     for event in stream:
L256:         if event.get("method") != "messages":
L257:             continue
L258: 
L259:         payload = event["params"]["data"][0]
L260:         if not isinstance(payload, dict):
L261:             continue
L262:         if payload.get("event") != "content-block-delta":
L263:             continue
L264: 
L265:         block = payload.get("delta") or {}
L266:         if block.get("type") == "text-delta":
L267:             source = "subagent" if event["params"]["namespace"] else "coordinator"
L268:             print(f"[{source}] {block['text']}")
L269:             text_deltas.append(block["text"])
L270:     `

L273: cite51†​ L274: 
L275: Subagents versus subgraphs
L276: 
L277: `stream.subgraphs` shows graph execution structure. `stream.subagents` shows product-level Deep Agents task delegations. Use `stream.subagents` for user-facing UI because it hides internal graph nodes and exposes the subagent concept directly.
